**Yes, you can deploy to production on a Friday afternoon, but it requires approval from the on-call engineering manager.**

The standard deployment window is **Monday through Thursday, 09:00–16:00 Pacific**. Friday deploys are not blocked outright—they just need that extra sign-off [1].

**Key details**
- Every deploy goes to a canary cell first (5% of traffic) and auto-promotes after 20 minutes if error rates and p95 latency stay within 10% of baseline [1].
- Rollbacks are always allowed at any time, without approval [1].
- The on-call engineering manager rotates; you can find the current on-call in PagerDuty or ask in `#eng-oncall`.

**When Friday deploys are *not* allowed**
- During the **holiday freeze** (Dec 18, 2026 – Jan 4, 2027) only standard and emergency changes are permitted [2].
- During the **month-end billing freeze** (last business day of the month until invoices are sent, usually the 2nd), normal changes to the Ledger service are blocked [2].

If you need a Friday deploy, ping the on-call engineering manager for approval before merging to `main`.

**Critical lab values must reach the ordering clinician within 60 minutes.** If you cannot reach the ordering clinician within **30 minutes**, the result is escalated to the **medical director on call** [1].

**Key points:**
- **60-minute deadline** – The critical result must be communicated to the clinician who ordered it within one hour.
- **30-minute escalation trigger** – If the ordering clinician is unreachable after 30 minutes, the result goes to the medical director on call.
- **Documentation required** – Every critical-result notification is recorded in the patient’s chart with the time and the name of the person notified [1].

**What to do if you can’t reach the ordering clinician:**
1. Continue attempts for up to 30 minutes.
2. At the 30-minute mark, contact the medical director on call and relay the critical value.
3. Document both the attempts to reach the ordering clinician and the hand-off to the medical director in the chart.

**287 workspaces** received duplicate invoices, and **$184,300** was refunded across 201 auto-charged invoices [1].

**Details from the incident (INC-2340):**
- The month-end invoicing job ran twice on October 6, creating 312 duplicate September invoices across 287 workspaces.
- 201 of those duplicate invoices were auto-charged to customers on card auto-pay.
- Harriet Vance (IDB change approver) directed the team to refund all 201 charges and void the remaining 111 unpaid duplicate invoices.
- Refunds totaling **$184,300** were issued the same day [1].

**17 lab results** were filed into the wrong patient's chart during the Bayline incident [1].

**Why it happened:**

1. **Bayline changed its results feed without notice** — On July 20, 2026, Bayline Reference Laboratories deployed a change that moved the medical record number (MRN) into a different HL7 segment, but did not inform Halcyon Health [1].

2. **The interface engine fell back to a weak matching rule** — When the MRN could no longer be found in its expected location, the Switchyard interface engine automatically switched to a secondary matching rule that had existed since 2021: matching on **last name and year of birth only**. This rule had never been exercised at volume before [1].

3. **No monitoring caught the problem** — There was no alerting when 100% of Bayline results began using the fallback match, so the issue went undetected for three days [1].

4. **Contractual gap** — The Bayline lab services agreement did not require advance notice of feed format changes [1].

The mismatch was discovered on July 23 when a medical assistant at Riverside noticed a potassium result that didn't match the patient's history. Two patients experienced delayed follow-up (4 and 6 days) due to abnormal results going to the wrong charts, but neither suffered lasting harm. All 17 results were moved to the correct charts by July 24 [1].
cited_titles: Root cause analysis: lab results filed to the wrong patient chart (RCA-26-07)

At Halcyon Health, the equivalent of a postmortem for a serious patient safety event is a **Root Cause Analysis (RCA)**. For the most severe events—**Level 1 Sentinel Events** (e.g., patient death or permanent harm unrelated to the natural course of illness, wrong‑patient/procedure, suicide within 72 hours of a visit)—the policy requires:

| Step | Deadline |
|------|----------|
| **RCA team chartered** by Quality & Patient Safety (QPS) | **Within 72 hours** of the event becoming known |
| **RCA completed** (with action plan) | **Within 45 calendar days** of the event becoming known |

The completed RCA, including its action plan, is then reviewed by the Patient Safety Committee (chaired by CMO Dr. Kenji Watanabe), which meets monthly and tracks every action item to closure [2].

So while a SEV‑1 postmortem is due in **5 business days**, Halcyon’s “really serious” (Level 1) patient safety events get a **45‑calendar‑day** window for the full RCA, with the team assembled within **3 days**.
cited_titles: Sentinel and adverse event reporting policy

At Halcyon Health clinics, the **charge nurse on shift** acts as the incident commander when something goes wrong with a patient. If no charge nurse is on shift, the **clinic manager** fills that role.

**What the charge nurse does immediately**  
- Coordinates the on‑scene response: assigns who stays with the patient, who contacts the family, and who secures any equipment, medications, or records involved.  
- For a sentinel event (patient death, permanent harm, wrong‑patient/procedure, etc.), notifies the on‑call medical director within **1 hour**.  

**Escalation path**  
1. Make the patient safe (follow the clinical escalation protocol; call 911 if needed).  
2. Alert the charge nurse (or clinic manager).  
3. The charge nurse runs the immediate response and, for sentinel events, escalates to the medical director.  
4. Anyone involved files a report in **SafeReport**; a root‑cause analysis follows for Level 1–2 events.  

So, while the term “incident commander” isn’t used verbatim in the policies, the charge nurse (or clinic manager) is the designated on‑site leader who directs the real‑time response to a patient safety event. [2]
cited_titles: Sentinel and adverse event reporting policy

**Halcyon Health requires four things before any vendor can receive or handle patient data (PHI):**

1. **A signed Business Associate Agreement (BAA)** — this is the HIPAA equivalent of a DPA. No PHI may be shared, even for a pilot or test file, until the BAA is fully executed [1].

2. **A completed security risk assessment** — the vendor must pass Halcyon’s security review (sometimes “with conditions”) before data flows [1][4][6].

3. **An entry in the Clinical and Business Systems Inventory** — the system/vendor must be listed on the approved inventory maintained by the HIPAA Security Officer [2][5].

4. **For clinical-use tools, a clinical safety review by the CMIO** — required when the vendor’s service touches clinical workflows (e.g., an AI scribe) [2].

**Yes, Northwind has an analogous “break-the-glass” mechanism, but it’s built for technical support rather than clinical care.**  

| Aspect | Halcyon Health – Break-the-glass EHR access | Northwind Labs – Emergency workspace access |
|--------|---------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------|
| **Purpose** | Open a patient’s chart outside your normal treatment relationship when care urgently requires it. | Enter a customer’s workspace to fix an urgent technical issue (pipeline down, connector broken, customer locked out). |
| **Who can use it** | All workforce members with Meridian EHR access (clinicians, covering providers, telehealth staff). | Support engineers, solutions engineers, on-call engineers. |
| **Trigger** | Unscheduled urgent patient, covering a colleague, telehealth escalation where the assigned clinician is unavailable. | An open support case **or** a declared incident that requires workspace access. “Curiosity” or “it would be faster” are explicitly not valid reasons. |
| **How to invoke** | In Meridian: click **Emergency access** → pick a reason (*Emergency care*, *Coverage*, *Other*) → type a short justification. | Run `nwctl access request --workspace <id> --reason <case-or-incident-id>`. |
| **Real-time approval** | **None** – patient care comes first; access is granted immediately. | **Mandatory** – a second engineer (from support/on-call, not on the same case) must approve in Teleport. You cannot approve your own request. |
| **Access level** | Full chart access for the patient in question. | **Read-only by default**. Write access (e.g., editing a pipeline) requires the customer’s written consent in the case first. |
| **Duration** | Until end of shift, max **12 hours**. Must re-break the glass if needed longer. | **2 hours** (deliberately shorter than the standard 8-hour Teleport session). Can re-request with a case update. |
| **Audit & review** | Every event logged; Privacy Officer’s team reviews within **2 business days**. Unclear reasons trigger manager confirmation. Inappropriate use = privacy incident (sanctions up to termination). | All sessions recorded. Quarterly access reviews by team leads; unconfirmed access is auto-revoked. Access revoked within 1 hour of departure. |
| **Governance owner** | Privacy Officer (Margaret Holloway) – HIPAA privacy policy. | Security team – Information Security Policy (Head of Security approves exceptions). |
| **Underlying principle** | “Minimum necessary” still applies; never for family, coworkers, VIPs, or self. | Access to customer data requires a ticket linked to a case/incident; standing access to production databases is prohibited for everyone. |

**In short:**  
- **Halcyon’s** is a *clinical safety valve* – no gatekeeper in the moment, heavy post-hoc privacy review.  
- **Northwind’s** is a *technical incident tool* – a mandatory two-person gate, short time-box, read-only default, and continuous session recording.

**No — at both organizations, putting sensitive data in Slack is explicitly prohibited.**

**Northwind Labs**  
- The Information Security Policy classifies customer event payloads, credentials, and encryption keys as **Restricted** data, which must *“never leaves production; never in tickets or Slack.”* [1]  
- The Emergency Access guide reinforces this: *“Restricted data never leaves production, so do not paste payloads into tickets, Slack, or a support reply.”* [4]

**Halcyon Health**  
- The Clinical & Business Systems Inventory lists Slack under **“Systems that must not hold PHI”** with the note **“Never, including DMs.”** [2]  
- The HIPAA Privacy & PHI Handling Policy states: *“Never put PHI in email subject lines, Slack, personal notes apps, or AI tools that are not on the approved list.”* [3]

**Bottom line:**  
- **Northwind:** No Restricted data (customer payloads, credentials, keys) in Slack.  
- **Halcyon:** No PHI in Slack, not even in direct messages.  

Use the approved, secure channels each organization provides (e.g., encrypted email with `[secure]` subject at Halcyon; production systems and secure ticketing at Northwind).

Changing the timing of medication reminder texts is considered a **significant change** to a patient-facing clinical system, so it requires a three-step approval chain:

1. **System steward approval** – The medication reminder scheduler (Pillbox) is owned by **Digital Health Engineering — Patient Engagement (DHE-PE)**, whose steward is **Felix Brandt** [2][4].
2. **Clinical safety sign-off** – The CMIO, **Dr. Anjali Rao** (or her delegate, Associate CMIO **Dr. Benedict Osei**) must sign off on the change [2].
3. **CSCAB review** – The weekly Clinical Systems Change Advisory Board (Wednesdays at 14:00 Eastern) must review and approve the change [2].

Halcyon treats patient-facing automation (like medication reminders) as a clinical system. The policy explicitly lists “patient-facing automation (reminders, outreach messages, the patient app’s clinical content)” as a trigger for the significant-change process [2]. A past incident (IR-0412) where a scheduler cutover caused duplicate reminders reinforced that any change to the reminder scheduler needs a written runbook and clinical safety sign-off [1].

**365 days** is the current default retention period for customers' archived event data.

This is set in the **Customer data retention standard v2** (effective September 15, 2026), which reduced the default archive retention from 400 days to **365 days** and renamed the cold store to **Driftwood** [2]. The standard specifies:

| Data | Where it lives | Default retention |
|------|----------------|-------------------|
| Archived event payloads | Driftwood | **365 days** |

Enterprise customers can contract for longer retention (up to 730 days) with security-team approval, but the default for all customers is 365 days [2].

**14 days** for all live systems. Backups continue to age out on their normal 35‑day schedule and are not restored for deleted data [1].

The current standard (v2, effective September 15 2026) reduced the deadline from the previous 30 days to **14 days** for verified deletion requests such as GDPR erasure [1]. Support logs each request in the `data‑requests` queue, which alerts at day 10 [1].

**Primary on-call pay for shifts starting in mid-November 2026:**

| Component | Amount |
|-----------|--------|
| Weekly stipend | **$500 per week** |
| Out-of-hours page | **$150 per page** |
| Weekly cap on page pay | **$1,500 per week** |

These rates take effect for on-call shifts starting on or after **Tuesday, November 3, 2026**, per the compensation update memo from VP Engineering Dmitri Sokolov and CFO Renata Kowal [1]. Mid-November shifts fall under this new structure.

*Previous rates (from the runbook) were $400/week stipend and $100 per out-of-hours page with no weekly cap [2].*

**56 hours** of unused annual leave can roll over into the next calendar year under the current policy effective October 1, 2026 [2].

**Key details:**
- The Annual Leave Policy (effective October 1, 2026) replaced the previous PTO policy and increased the carry-over limit from 40 hours to **56 hours** [2].
- Any unused annual leave above 56 hours is paid out in January at your current rate [2].
- The first carry-over under the new 56-hour limit will occur on **January 1, 2027** [2].
- Accrual rates remain unchanged: 6.15 hours per pay period (20 days/year) in years 1–3, and 7.7 hours per pay period (25 days/year) from year 4 onward [2].

Enterprise customers can use reference tables up to **500 million rows per workspace** with Tributary [2]. 

For comparison, the Growth plan supports up to 50 million rows per workspace [2].

The new telehealth platform (codenamed **Juniper**) has a two-phase rollout for patients:

| Phase | Date | Scope |
|-------|------|-------|
| **Pilot** | **January 12, 2027** | Riverside, Elm Park, and Northgate clinics only |
| **Network-wide** | **March 2, 2027** | All clinics and the telehealth front desk |

The pilot go/no-go decision will be made at the **December 16, 2026** steering committee meeting. Criteria include sustained join-success rates above 98%, zero open Level 1–2 safety findings, and CSCAB approval as a significant change [1].

The current vendor, Larkspur Telehealth, will remain on a month-to-month extension through **March 31, 2027**, after which it will be fully decommissioned [1][3].

**No — the Head of Security has not signed off yet.**

**Current status of RFC-031 (Persisting Tributary snapshots):**
- **Author:** L. Zhou (Lin Zhou / LZ), created September 18, 2026
- **Status:** Accepted with conditions
- **Security reviewer:** Tomasz Wierzbicki (Head of Security, initials **TW**)
- **TW's decision:** ⏳ **Pending** — wants a threat model for copying Restricted data across tiers before approving [1]

**Key context:**
- The RFC explicitly states: *"Implementation can start behind a flag, but nothing ships to the private beta until TW signs off."* [1]
- Leadership offsite notes from October 1 confirm: *"Dmitri noted security sign-off on persisted snapshots is still outstanding and is the main risk."* [3]
- An action item from that offsite tasked Dmitri to *"unblock the RFC-031 security review with Tomasz by end of October"* [3], but as of the latest records the review remains pending.

**Other approvals:**
- Priya Raman (Data Plane) ✅ Approved Sep 22
- Oluwaseun Adeyemi (Platform) ✅ Approved with conditions Sep 24 (snapshots must go in a separate Driftwood bucket) [1]

Until Tomasz Wierzbicki provides the threat model review and approves, the feature cannot ship to the private beta.

The self-serve billing portal (codenamed **Lantern**) has slipped from its original timeline. As of the October 1 leadership offsite:

- **Beta launch:** February 2027 (moved from December 2026)  
- **General availability (GA):** March 2027 (moved from January 2027) [2]

The delay is because the payment-provider migration won't finish until mid-January 2027, and the invoice-history view needs to properly handle voided invoices (a lesson from INC-2340) [2].

The final ARR for Q4 2026 isn't available yet—Q4 hasn't ended, and the leadership team noted that the Q4 numbers "will be finalized for the December board meeting" [2].

The most recent actual figure reported is **$18.4M ARR at the end of Q3 2026** (up 9% quarter-over-quarter and 41% year-over-year) [1]. The October leadership offsite discussed a Q4 forecast—including a likely renewal of a $640K logistics contract—but those numbers were still in draft form [2].

The knowledge base doesn't specify how many weeks of paid parental leave Northwind Labs provides. The only reference to parental leave is in the October 2026 leadership offsite notes, which note that "Joanne presented the parental leave benchmarking. Decision deferred to the December meeting; no change to the current policy yet" [1]. This confirms a policy exists, but the documents don't state its details. The onboarding guide lists other benefits (health coverage, 401(k) match, learning budget, home-office stipend, flexible PTO) but does not mention parental leave [2].

There is no entry for Bayline Reference Laboratories, so I can't provide a BAA renewal date for that vendor. If Bayline operates under a different legal name or is tracked in another system, you may need to check with the vendor management team or the Privacy Officer.

The Halcyon Health knowledge base does not contain a travel expense policy or any document that specifies a daily meal allowance (per diem) for staff traveling for training.

What I did find:
- Clinical staff receive **$2,000 per year for continuing medical education (CME)** and **5 days of paid CME time** [1], but the documents don't break this down into daily meal rates or travel per diems.
- The available policies cover onboarding, PTO/annual leave, sick leave, HIPAA training, and billing FAQs—none address business travel reimbursement or meal allowances.

If you need the current meal allowance, you may need to check with the People team or Finance for a separate travel and expense policy that isn't in this knowledge base.
